"In the sweltering heat of Darwin, the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, a tragic tale unfolded, one that would eventually reveal a systemic failure within the local police force. The story began to unravel on the 16th of September last year, when two police officers, en route to a noise complaint, stumbled upon a grim scene. A Toyota Hilux had met its match in a sturdy palm tree, its crumpled remains steaming in the tropical air. Hidden amongst the vegetation, a young man named Dale Scott Walkinshaw cradled his injured passenger, a woman he had met earlier that evening at a local bar.

Walkinshaw, though unharmed, was significantly over the legal blood alcohol limit, registering a reading of 0.149. His passenger, however, was not so lucky. She drifted in and out of consciousness, having sustained a serious back injury. The stage was set for a tragedy that would shine a harsh light on the shortcomings of the Northern Territory police.

In the days and weeks that followed, the scrutiny intensified. It emerged that this was not the first time such an incident had occurred. In fact, the Northern Territory police had been criticized years prior for inaction following a string of self-harm incidents and suicide attempts in the back of their caged vehicles. Between 2013 and the fateful night of Walkinshaw's arrest, there had been at least 16 attempted suicides in these vehicles. Six of these individuals were not found until they were semi-conscious or unconscious.

The coroner, Greg Cavanagh, was scathing in his assessment. He found that it was not a matter of 'if' but 'when' a person would die in the back of a police van. He criticized the police for their failure to act on an internal report from 2013, which had recommended the installation of CCTV cameras in these vehicles. This recommendation had come after a previous death in custody, yet the police had failed to implement it.

The story sent shockwaves through the community, sparking a public outcry and demands for reform. The Northern Territory police were forced to confront their failures, to look into the eyes of their demons and acknowledge the lives lost on their watch. The death of Dale Scott Walkinshaw, the vulnerable 23-year-old, would not be in vain. His tragic story would serve as a catalyst for change, a stark reminder of the need for vigilance and accountability within our institutions."
